common_mistakes: Submitting the clinic as a generic office TI and leaving out medical gas and X-ray equipment review — that usually gets bounced in plan review
Assuming the plumbing sinks can be covered under the building permit only — the plumbing rough-in needs its own permit and inspection
Treating medical gas like ordinary HVAC or plumbing — it needs specialized review, testing, and documentation
Forgetting the electrical load and dedicated circuit requirements for X-ray equipment, which can trigger redesign after plan review starts
Starting tenant improvement demolition before the permit is issued and posted — Mesa can stop the job and require corrections before work continues
Forgetting exam-room sinks, fixture counts, backflow/indirect waste, or accessible restroom upgrades in the plumbing scope.
Leaving medical gas, nitrous/oxygen, alarms, zone valves, and verifier paperwork out of the permit package.
Using ordinary office HVAC assumptions instead of confirming ventilation, exhaust, pressure relationships, filtration, and infection-control needs for procedure/sterilization/lab rooms.
Missing ADA path-of-travel documentation for reception, exam rooms, restrooms, route, parking/passenger loading, and check-in counters.

pro_tips: Bundle the building, plumbing, mechanical/medical gas, and electrical submittals together so Mesa can coordinate plan review instead of sending you through multiple correction cycles
Have the X-ray equipment cut sheet and any shielding/anchorage details ready before submittal — that is where commercial clinic jobs often stall
If the medical gas system is being altered, get the installer and testing documentation lined up early; inspectors will want pressure test and labeling details before final
Mesa uses Accela, so make sure the contractor account is active before you start the application — login issues can delay the whole TI package
For commercial TI work, verify the tenant space address and suite number exactly match the lease and plans; Mesa plan review is strict about suite identification

Treat medical clinic TI as a specialty commercial buildout, not a plain office: confirm exam-room plumbing, medical gas, infection-control/HVAC, accessibility, fire/life-safety, and health-care licensing paths before pricing.

Ask the owner early whether the clinic includes x-ray/radiology, oxygen/nitrous/medical gas, sterilization, lab work, procedure rooms, or state-licensed health-care services — each can add separate reviews.
Coordinate architect/MEP, medical-gas verifier, equipment vendor, and health/licensing reviewer before submitting so room names, fixture schedules, ventilation, and equipment utility loads match.
Likely outpatient Business Group B clinic basis, but verify B vs I-2/ambulatory-care status with the building department if any procedure, sedation, recovery, or self-preservation issue exists.

watch_out: A clinic with exam rooms, treatment rooms, medical gas, or x-ray can be rejected if submitted as generic office TI with only building/electrical scope.
Health-care licensing or state/local health review may control opening even after the building permit is final; verify this path before promising an opening date.
Medical gas and x-ray shielding often need specialty documentation and third-party verification; missing it can block final inspection or equipment operation.
response_body.zoning_hoa_flag: Commercial tenant improvements can still be delayed by zoning, use, or occupancy issues if the suite use changes, parking counts are affected, or the medical clinic use triggers a different occupancy classification. HOA restrictions are usually not the issue for a commercial clinic TI, but any exterior signage, rooftop equipment, or exterior alterations may need separate review. If the X-ray equipment requires shielding or exterior venting, verify with Mesa Development Services before ordering materials.
